title: The Life-Changing Magic of Tidying Up

facts.claim: Japanese original Jinsei ga Tokimeku Katazuke no Maho (Sunmark, 2011); English edition The Life-Changing Magic of Tidying Up (Ten Speed Press, 2014).
Selection criterion: keep only what sparks joy; 'whether or not it gives you a thrill of pleasure when you touch it.' Each item is taken in hand.
'Keep things because you love them, not just because.' People hold on out of 'an attachment to the past or a fear for the future.'

Items that no longer spark joy are thanked before being let go: a gift has done its job when it was received; an item bought but not used gave joy when bought and has completed its role ('Thank you for giving me joy when I bought you').
Discarding comes before deciding where to store. 'Tidying up by location is a fatal mistake': items of the same kind are scattered across rooms.
Order: clothes first, then books, papers, komono (miscellany), and lastly mementos/sentimental items. Moving from easier to harder decisions; sentimental items and photos come last.
All items of one category are gathered in one place before deciding (e.g. every piece of clothing in the house on the floor).
facts.source: widely summarized; not quoted verbatim in accessed sources

facts.claim: Numerical goals ('seven jackets and ten blouses is the perfect amount') are one reason other methods result in rebound.
Kondo worked five years as a Shinto shrine maiden (miko).

Kondo greets a client's house before tidying: 'I began this custom quite naturally based on the etiquette of worshipping at Shinto shrines'; the moment a client opens the door 'resembles the atmosphere when one passes under a shrine gate'; 'my way of showing respect for the house and its contents.' She kneels in the centre of the house and greets it in her mind.
'I began to treat my belongings as if they were alive when I was a high school student.'
When she comes home she greets her house and, as she puts down her handbag, thanks it for the day's work.
'Just like the gentle shake we use to wake someone up, we can stimulate our belongings by physically moving them.'
'Clutter is caused by a failure to return things to where they belong.' 'Store all items of the same type in the same place.'
Kondo began thinking about storage at age five and discovered discarding as a teenager.
Kondo also phrases the joy test as 'speak to your heart' or 'moves you'.

'Tidying is just a tool, not the final destination.' 'After tidying, many clients tell me that their worldly desires have decreased.' Three approaches: 'face them now, face them sometime, or avoid them until the day we die.'
Kondo visited her community shrine often as a child; the greeting can be spoken aloud or silently.

rejected.claim: Dialogue with a client holding an old blouse ('Do you feel joy holding it?' / 'I only keep it because I paid for it').
rejected.reason: Scene not found in the book; invented.

rejected.claim: 'Does this give you energy or take it away?' as Kondo's method.
rejected.reason: Not the book's wording; criterion is joy when touching.

rejected.claim: 'Thank your bag as you enter it' and that the method spreads to relationships, habits and work ('Does this relationship spark joy?').
'Every photo takes ten minutes' and 'decision muscle' wording.
'Clutter comes from postponed decisions, not too many objects' as Kondo's line.
rejected.reason: Not her wording; she says clutter comes from failure to return things to their place.
